analysis.one_liner: Removes dollar caps on damages awarded to victims of workplace discrimination.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 34 bipartisan cosponsors, was referred to the Senate labor committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 1991 Civil Rights Act let workers win compensatory and punitive damages for intentional job discrimination, but capped those awards based on how many employees their employer has, from $50,000 at the smallest firms up to $300,000 at the largest. This bill would erase those caps so every victim of discrimination could recover full damages no matter how big their employer is, and would guarantee a jury trial on demand in these cases.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face intentional discrimination on the job because of race, sex, religion, national origin, or disability. Under current law their monetary awards are capped by their employer's size; the bill would let courts award whatever compensatory and punitive damages the case warrants, and give any party the right to a jury trial. Workers at small and mid-sized companies, who face the lowest caps, would gain the most.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the statutory dollar limits on awards for out-of-pocket losses, emotional harm, and punitive damages in intentional employment discrimination cases.
Equalizes remedies so that a discrimination victim's recovery does not depend on how many employees their employer has, as it does under the caps added by the Civil Rights Act of 1991.
Adds a right for any party in these cases to demand a jury trial rather than have a judge decide damages.

analysis.who_pays: Employers found liable for intentional discrimination, who would face potentially unlimited jury awards instead of the current caps, and their insurers. Businesses would also bear the cost of longer, jury-based litigation.

drawbacks.text: Removing all caps exposes employers of every size, including small businesses that currently face the lowest caps, to unlimited compensatory and punitive awards decided by juries, which raises the cost and unpredictability of litigation.

Supporters of the 1991 caps argued they were a compromise that made new damages remedies possible at all; eliminating them reopened a settled bargain and risked a political fight that could endanger the existing remedy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a worker harmed by deliberate discrimination, uncapped damages means the remedy can actually match the injury, and a small company's victim is no longer compensated less than a victim at a big corporation. The cost falls on employers, who would face greater and less predictable liability; whether that cost is excessive or simply the true price of discrimination is the core disagreement the bill never got to resolve.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took action on it, and it died when the 103rd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Kennedy introduced the bill on January 21, 1993, with 34 cosponsors including 4 Republicans.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
No further action was recorded: no hearings, no markup, no floor vote, through the end of the 103rd Congress on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, particularly those that would have faced uncapped damages awards for intentional discrimination, are better off that the bill never advanced. Discrimination victims remain under the size-based caps set by the 1991 Civil Rights Act.

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Equal Remedies Act of 1993 to lift the damages caps on employment discrimination awards.

for.name: 34 senators, including 4 Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including Republican senators Durenberger, Packwood, Cohen, and Specter.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled hearings, a markup, or a vote; the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan: 30 of the 34 cosponsors were Democrats and 4 were Republicans, and the bill's opposition is not visible in the record because the committee simply never acted.

industries.industry: Employers subject to federal anti-discrimination law
industries.note: The bill would end the size-based caps that limit what an employer must pay a worker it intentionally discriminated against, exposing businesses to unlimited jury awards. Employers' interest in keeping those caps runs directly against discrimination victims' interest in full compensation.
Uncapped, jury-decided awards would mean more litigation and larger settlements, increasing demand for defense lawyers and raising employers' discrimination insurance costs.
